summary: Maintain the k-th largest element as numbers stream in.
mainInsight: You only ever need the k largest values: keep them in a min-heap of size k whose root is the k-th largest; a new value matters only if it beats the root.

approaches.name: Sort on every add
approaches.timeComplexity: O(n log n) per add (O(n) on nearly sorted)
approaches.interviewRelevance: Your approach: correct but not optimal.

approaches.name: Min-heap of size k
approaches.summary: Push, pop when size > k; root = k-th largest.

personalSolution.approach: Append and sort on every add
personalSolution.notes: Correct but slow. Use a min-heap of size k for O(log k) updates.

promptVariants: Why is a MIN-heap used to track the k LARGEST elements?
Why can everything below the k-th largest be discarded?
cards.answer: The element that would be displaced next is the smallest of the current top k, so it must be at the root. Elements smaller than the k-th largest can never become the k-th largest later (new values only push the threshold up), so they can be discarded.
keyPoints: Root = smallest of the top k

promptVariants: Your solution keeps all numbers. What does the heap version store and why is it enough?
Compare the memory of the two approaches.
cards.answer: Yours stores every number O(n) and re-sorts on each add. The heap keeps only the k largest, O(k), which is sufficient because no smaller number can ever be the k-th largest again.
keyPoints: Smaller values can never matter again
cards.explanation: The constructor must heapify then trim to size k.
cards.code:
class KthLargest:

    def __init__(self, k: int, nums: List[int]):
        self.heap = nums[:]
        self.k = k

    def add(self, val: int) -> int:
        self.heap.append(val)

        self.heap.sort()
        return self.heap[-self.k]


# Your KthLargest object will be instantiated and called as such:
# obj = KthLargest(k, nums)
# param_1 = obj.add(val)

promptVariants: Your add appends and sorts the whole list. What is the cost and how would a size-k heap change `__init__` and `add`?
cards.code:
def add(self, val):
    self.heap.append(val)
    self.heap.sort()
    return self.heap[-self.k]
cards.answer: Sorting costs O(n log n) per call (Timsort is nearly linear on almost-sorted data but still O(n)). With a heap: __init__ heapifies and pops until size <= k; add does heappush(val) and, if len > k, heappop(), then returns heap[0].
keyPoints: Sort per add is O(n log n)
push, pop if > k, return heap[0]
cards.explanation: The list called `heap` is not actually a heap in your code - naming matters.
